cta.title: Clean your air
cta.desc: Take absolute control of your indoor environment. Precise, real-time tracking for CO2, particulate matter, temperature, and humidity.

index.hero_title: Your home warns you before El Niño does
index.hero_lead: A low-cost neighborhood station that measures heat, humidity and air inside your home and, with AI, tells you today's risk (dengue, heat stroke, humidity) and what to do, citing official sources.
index.problem_title: El Niño gets inside the home too
index.problem_desc: More intense heat, heavy rain on the northern coast and stagnant water. Official bulletins exist, but they don't reach the home or say what to do today.
index.dengue_desc: Rain leaves stagnant water where the Aedes aegypti mosquito breeds.
index.heat_desc: Children and older adults are the most exposed to heat inside the home.
index.humidity_desc: Sustained high humidity brings mold and breathing problems.
index.problem_stat: In 2023, with the coastal El Niño and Cyclone Yaku, Peru's CDC warned of a dengue epidemic: 72,163 cases and 79 deaths reported by epidemiological week 18 alone.
index.how_desc: From a reading inside the home to a one-line warning any family understands.
index.step1_desc: Temperature, humidity, CO₂ and particles inside the home, every few minutes.
index.step2_desc: A 0–100 risk index for dengue, heat and humidity, explained in one sentence.
index.step3_desc: A plain-language warning with one concrete action for today.
index.step4_desc: An emergency assistant that answers from official guides and cites the source.
index.ai_title: AI that turns data into action
index.ai_desc: Not just a chatbot: AI interprets what is happening in your home, writes the alert and answers with official sources.
index.ai1_desc: Evidence-based rules (mosquito range, heat index) plus a language model that explains the result in one sentence.
index.ai2_desc: "Humidity 84%" becomes a clear warning with a concrete action, ready to share with the community.
index.ai3_desc: Answers only from official MINSA and INDECI guides, cites the source and says so when it doesn't know.
index.alert_text: “The heat and humidity inside your home favor the breeding of the dengue mosquito. Empty standing water from buckets, tanks and containers today. Follow official MINSA and SENAMHI alerts.” (translated from the Spanish original)
index.kit_desc: Low-cost, off-the-shelf hardware, designed to be installed in a home or across the neighborhood.
index.kit_sht40: Temperature and humidity for the heat index and dengue risk.
index.kit_scd41: CO₂ to know when to ventilate the home.
index.kit_pm: PM2.5 and PM10 particles in the air.
index.kit_rain: Tipping-bucket rain gauge that measures accumulated rainfall.
index.kit_level: Ultrasonic or radar sensor to anticipate floods and mudslides (huaicos).
index.kit_esp32: Processes the readings and sends them over Wi-Fi.
index.kit_case: Outdoor-ready, with battery and optional solar panel.
index.muni_desc: With several stations in a neighborhood, municipalities will be able to prioritize where to fumigate or send help first.
index.disclaimer: Guidance estimate only. Always follow official alerts from SENAMHI, INDECI and MINSA.

about.hero_img_alt: Bedroom in a Chaclacayo house covered in mud after Cyclone Yaku, March 2023
about.hero_credit: Bedroom in Chaclacayo after Cyclone Yaku, March 2023 · MapacheVioleta, CC0
about.hero_title: El Niño reaches the house. So do we.
about.hero_subtitle: We are Mateo Aleman Romano, Victor Nicolas Ortiz, Ian Macavilca and Neil Andrew Quripaco. Clair Niño exists so a coastal family can tell, today, whether the heat and humidity inside their home favor the mosquito or heat illness.
about.why_title: The Pacific warms. The warning stays in the bulletin.
about.why_desc: When El Niño warms the sea off Peru, the northern coast gets heavier rain, nights that do not cool, and still water in yards and buckets. SENAMHI, INDECI and MINSA publish the alert. In a kitchen in Piura, that alert still does not say what to do this afternoon.
about.why_img_alt: Interior of a Chaclacayo home with mud after Cyclone Yaku
about.why_credit: Home in Chaclacayo, March 2023 · MapacheVioleta, CC0
about.memory_title: We saw it in the river, not on a slide.
about.memory_desc: The 2017 coastal El Niño swelled the Piura River into the city. In 2023, with another coastal El Niño and Cyclone Yaku, dengue filled the epidemiological weeks again. Clair Niño comes from that memory: the phenomenon does not end at sea. It ends in the house.
about.memory_img_alt: Houses in Babahoyo, Ecuador, surrounded by water during El Niño
about.memory_credit: Babahoyo, Ecuador, during El Niño · Etinar, CC BY-SA 4.0
about.team_desc: Four people, four pieces. None of them works alone: the reading, the screen, the emergency sentence, and the story told outside the app.
about.team_alt: Mateo Aleman Romano, Victor Nicolas Ortiz, Ian Macavilca and Neil Andrew Quripaco
about.mateo_role: The Niño Mode screen. Makes today's risk visible so a family does not have to read a dashboard.
about.nicolas_role: The alert. Turns humidity and heat into a short sentence, and keeps a fallback line if the model does not answer.
about.ian_role: The emergency assistant. Answers from MINSA and INDECI guidance, cites the source, and says so when it is not in the guides.
about.neil_role: The story. Landing, pitch and video so El Niño is understood before the app is opened.

product.hero_title: The station that listens to the house during El Niño
product.hero_lead: It measures heat, humidity, CO₂ and particles inside the home. From that it scores today's risk and writes a plain-language alert, citing MINSA and SENAMHI.
product.risk_title: The rain is measured outside. The risk is decided inside.
product.risk_desc: A rain gauge counts what falls. Inside the house, heat and humidity say whether that rain left still water where the mosquito breeds. Clair Niño joins both readings and turns them into a sentence for today.
product.gauge_alt: A weighing rain gauge installed outdoors
product.gauge_credit: Ott Pluvio2 rain gauge, Viikki · Antti Leppänen, CC BY 4.0
product.station_title: From a reading to a single action
product.station_desc: The station does not ask you to interpret a chart. It delivers one line: empty the standing water, ventilate, look after whoever suffers the heat most, and follow the official warning.
product.specs_header: What it measures when El Niño tightens
product.heat_desc: The SHT40 records the temperature and humidity used for the heat index and for the range that favors the mosquito.
product.air_desc: The SCD41 says when to ventilate because of CO₂. The particle sensor follows PM2.5 and PM10 when dust and smoke stay indoors.
product.water_desc: A tipping-bucket gauge measures what falls. A level sensor watches water rising toward a flood or a huaico, before it reaches the door.
product.link_desc: An ESP32 processes the sensors and sends them over Wi-Fi. An IP65 case handles the outdoors, with a battery and optional solar panel if the neighborhood loses power.
product.place_title: Built for the coast El Niño keeps visiting
product.place_desc: Piura, Máncora, and any house where summer stops being only heat. Start with one station. With several, a municipality sees first where to fumigate or whom to warn.
product.place_alt: Houses in Babahoyo surrounded by water during El Niño
product.place_credit: Babahoyo, Ecuador, during El Niño · Etinar, CC BY-SA 4.0
product.cta_desc: Buying the station is the first step. What reaches the family is a sentence for today, with the source beside it.
